worldSentence: The Gulf's emergency energy routes are now targets themselves: Saudi Arabia shut its east-west pipeline after drone strikes, the Houthis expanded beside Bab el-Mandeb, and another ship was hit near Hormuz.
standfirst: The system built to route around a dangerous Strait of Hormuz is being tested at both ends. Saudi Arabia shut its east-west oil pipeline after drones launched from Iraq struck facilities in Riyadh and Medina provinces; the Houthis say they now hold Mokha and an island inside Bab el-Mandeb; and an Iranian cargo ship was hit near Hormuz. The economic transmission is visible in August U.S. consumer inflation, which reached 3.4% as gasoline, airfares and lodging climbed. Elsewhere, Ukraine enters winter with a widening fiscal and export squeeze, BRICS agreed to deepen local-currency payment links without creating a common currency, India and China attempted a political reset, and rival AI chiefs converged on a proposal for embedded external evaluators.

connected.title: Every bypass is part of the system now—and therefore part of the target set.

signals.label: SAUDI BYPASS
signals.text: Saudi Arabia halted the east-west pipeline after drone strikes on facilities in Riyadh and Medina provinces.

signals.label: HORMUZ
signals.text: Commercial movement remains depressed as regional ministers prepare to discuss traffic management in Oman.

signals.label: U.S. CPI
signals.text: August consumer inflation accelerated, with gasoline accounting for more than one-third of the monthly increase.

connected.note: The Saudi east-west pipeline exists to move crude from Gulf fields to Yanbu on the Red Sea when Hormuz is constrained. That redundancy only works if the western coast and the land bridge remain secure. Drone strikes forced the pipeline's precautionary shutdown while the Houthi advance increased risk around Bab el-Mandeb. An Iranian cargo ship was separately hit near Hormuz, where traffic is still low. These are confirmed disruptions, but not proof of a coordinated campaign against every alternative route. The immediate commercial effect is higher uncertainty around capacity, timing and insurance; the macro effect is already spreading through gasoline, airfares and accommodation.

stories.title: Saudi Arabia shut its Hormuz bypass as the Houthis expanded beside Bab el-Mandeb and another ship was hit near Hormuz.
stories.changed: Saudi Arabia said drones launched from Iraq struck energy facilities in Riyadh and Medina provinces on Thursday, injuring workers and prompting a precautionary shutdown of the east-west oil pipeline to Yanbu. Iraq confirmed a launch site in Maysan, removed the local operations commander and opened an investigation. By Sunday, the Houthis had taken Mokha and said they controlled an island inside Bab el-Mandeb, while an Iranian cargo ship was hit near Hormuz, killing one person and wounding four according to Iranian media. Responsibility for the ship strike is unconfirmed.
stories.matters: The east-west pipeline is Saudi Arabia's principal physical hedge against Hormuz disruption. Its shutdown means a route designed as redundancy has become an operational vulnerability at the same time the Red Sea exit is exposed to an expanding Houthi campaign. This does not mean Saudi exports have stopped or that Bab el-Mandeb is closed. It means planners, traders and insurers must price correlated failure across a network that was assumed to offer independent alternatives.
stories.watch: When Saudi Arabia restarts the pipeline; evidence from the Iraqi investigation; any Saudi response; verified Houthi control of the island and new shipping warnings; commercial transit counts at both straits; the condition of Yanbu infrastructure; responsibility for the Iranian ship strike; and Monday's Oman meeting on traffic management, including whether it produces practical guarantees rather than declarations.

group.label: The lead
group.title: The fallback network has become the battlefield.
group.note: The pipeline shutdown and Iraqi launch site are confirmed. Coordination between the attacks, permanent damage and control of the straits are not established.

background.title: Redundancy fails when its supposedly separate risks become correlated
background.text: Saudi Arabia's Petroline carries crude west across the kingdom to Yanbu, allowing exports to avoid Hormuz. From Yanbu, cargoes still depend on the Red Sea route through Bab el-Mandeb. That architecture separates an eastern chokepoint from a western outlet, but it does not eliminate geography: the land pipeline can be struck, the terminal can be threatened and ships still need a narrow southern exit. The latest events touched all three layers within days. The analytical mistake would be to call the network closed; the operating mistake would be to treat each event as isolated before restart timing, damage and adversary intent are known.
background.known: Saudi facilities were struck by drones launched from Iraq, the pipeline was shut as a precaution, and the Houthis expanded around Mokha.
background.new: The main physical workaround for Hormuz is temporarily unavailable while both maritime exits carry active security risk.

left.label: Confirmed floor
left.text: Saudi and Iraqi authorities confirmed the drone origin and shutdown; AP confirmed the Houthi territorial expansion through local sources.

right.label: Uncertain ceiling
right.text: No public evidence yet proves a unified campaign, lasting pipeline damage or an ability to close either strait.

Saudi Press Agency · drone origin and response posture
AP · Houthi expansion, displacement and Bab el-Mandeb risk
AP · Iranian cargo ship struck near Hormuz

stories.title: U.S. inflation accelerated to 3.4%, and markets moved toward expecting a rate increase next week.
stories.changed: The consumer price index rose 0.4% in August and 3.4% from a year earlier. Gasoline increased 3.9% and accounted for more than one-third of the monthly rise. Core inflation was 0.3% on the month and eased to 2.4% annually from 2.5%. Travel-sensitive categories moved sharply: airfares rose 2.7% in August and 23.4% over the year, while lodging rose 2.4% in one month. Rate futures implied roughly an 85% probability of a Federal Reserve increase at its September 15–16 meeting, according to Reuters.
stories.matters: The report is hotter in the categories households notice and more mixed underneath. Core annual inflation eased, but a fresh energy surge is lifting transport and travel costs before the full September shock enters the data. For the Fed, that combination raises the cost of waiting even though higher rates cannot create fuel supply. For airlines, hotels and restaurants, the same headline masks different exposure: travel prices can rise with constrained capacity, while food-away-from-home prices rose a more modest 0.3%.
stories.watch: The Fed's vote and projections; whether officials describe a hike as insurance or the start of a cycle; gasoline and diesel prices; inflation expectations; September airfare and lodging data; full-service restaurant pricing; Treasury yields; and signs that households reduce discretionary travel or dining rather than absorb the increase.

group.label: Economy and markets
group.title: Energy is lifting the headline faster than the core trend.
group.note: The CPI is measured data. The probability of a rate increase is a market price, not a decision by the Federal Reserve.

background.title: One inflation report can contain both a shock and a cooling trend
background.text: Headline CPI includes volatile food and energy prices; core CPI removes them to expose broader persistence. In August, gasoline drove much of the acceleration while annual core inflation edged lower. Yet the boundary is porous. Fuel enters freight, air travel and household expectations, while airfare and lodging can also reflect capacity and demand. The Fed must decide whether the shock will fade or alter wider price-setting. That is why the monthly composition and expectations matter more than treating 3.4% as a single verdict.
background.known: August headline inflation accelerated and gasoline, airfare and lodging all increased.
background.new: Core annual inflation eased slightly even as markets assigned a higher chance to an immediate rate increase.

left.label: Pressure
left.text: CPI rose 0.4% monthly; gasoline rose 3.9%; airfares were 23.4% higher than a year earlier.

right.label: Restraint
right.text: Core annual inflation eased to 2.4%, and a futures probability does not bind policymakers.

sources.label: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics · August CPI report
AP · inflation composition and household impact
Reuters · rate-futures response to CPI

stories.title: Trump asked Ukraine to stop striking Russian diesel infrastructure as U.S. pump prices rose above six dollars.
stories.changed: President Donald Trump said he asked President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries and fuel infrastructure, arguing that the strikes were adding to U.S. diesel prices that averaged above $6 a gallon on Friday. Russia has rationed fuel in some regions and restricted diesel exports after repeated Ukrainian attacks. Global prices also reflect the Iran war and impaired Gulf shipping, so the size of Ukraine's independent contribution is not established.
stories.matters: The request exposes a direct conflict between Ukraine's battlefield strategy and a sponsor's domestic price politics. Kyiv targets refining and logistics to reduce Russian war capacity and revenue; Washington now sees the same campaign through inflation and voter pressure. If U.S. support becomes conditional on energy-market restraint, Moscow gains protection for economically important infrastructure without conceding militarily. If Kyiv refuses, it risks political friction while entering a difficult winter.
stories.watch: Ukraine's public response and subsequent strike pattern; any U.S. linkage to weapons or intelligence; Russian refinery throughput and regional rationing; diesel exports; U.S. pump prices; whether Moscow reciprocates by limiting attacks on Ukrainian energy; and independent estimates separating Gulf disruption from lost Russian refining capacity.

group.label: War and political economy
group.title: A tactical pressure campaign collided with a sponsor's inflation constraint.
group.note: Trump's request and elevated diesel prices are confirmed. Causation is shared across multiple supply shocks and cannot be assigned to Ukraine alone.

background.title: Refineries translate crude oil into the products economies actually use
background.text: Destroying or disabling a refinery can leave crude production intact while reducing diesel, gasoline and jet-fuel output. That makes refineries militarily attractive and economically contagious targets. Russia can redirect crude exports more easily than it can instantly replace damaged processing equipment, while product shortages can affect logistics and military operations. But fuel markets are global: restrictions at Hormuz, shipping insurance, maintenance and inventories all influence the same price. A political request to stop attacks therefore rests on a plausible mechanism but an uncertain share of responsibility.
background.known: Ukraine has repeatedly struck Russian fuel infrastructure, Russia has constrained exports, and U.S. diesel prices rose sharply.
background.new: The U.S. president publicly asked Kyiv to change that military strategy because of domestic fuel prices.

left.label: Strategic logic
left.text: Russian rationing and export controls show that refinery attacks have constrained product availability.

right.label: Attribution limit
right.text: The Gulf war and shipping disruption are simultaneous drivers, so Ukraine's price contribution is not isolated.

sources.label: AP · Trump request, diesel prices and Russian fuel constraints

stories.title: Ukraine enters winter with damaged infrastructure, an effective port blockade and defense spending above domestic funding.
stories.changed: Reuters reported Ukrainian estimates of about $10 billion in 2026 damage to infrastructure and fixed assets, with the disruption subtracting roughly 1.5 percentage points from growth. An effective blockade of Black Sea ports puts about $40 billion of annual export revenue at risk. Domestic revenue fell about $1.35 billion short in the first eight months, while defense spending reached $42 billion against $39 billion from domestic revenue and local borrowing. Officials put the daily cost of the war near $190 million, up from $140 million in 2024.
stories.matters: The winter problem is a balance-sheet system, not only a heating problem. Damaged power and transport reduce output; blocked ports weaken foreign-currency earnings; weaker revenue increases reliance on external finance; and defense absorbs resources before reconstruction. Each constraint makes the others harder to solve. A funding delay can therefore become an energy, currency or logistics failure even without a decisive battlefield shift.
stories.watch: Emergency financing commitments and disbursement dates; Black Sea vessel movements and insurance; power-generation availability; gas storage and imports; budget revisions; the exchange rate; export rerouting costs; air-defense supply; and whether allies finance civilian resilience separately from military aid.

group.label: Ukraine's winter
group.title: Military endurance now depends on keeping the fiscal-export-energy loop intact.
group.note: The estimates come from Ukrainian officials and Reuters calculations; wartime damage and output are difficult to measure precisely.

background.title: A wartime budget can fail through timing before it fails in annual totals
background.text: Ukraine spends continuously on defense, wages, repairs and imported energy while tax and export receipts arrive unevenly. External support often comes in tranches subject to political approval. When ports are blocked, exporters earn less foreign currency and the state collects less revenue; when infrastructure is damaged, repair imports and social needs increase. Even if allies eventually cover the annual gap, delayed cash can force domestic borrowing, currency pressure or deferred maintenance at the worst seasonal moment.
background.known: Russian attacks have damaged energy and logistics assets while defense expenditure exceeds domestically raised resources.
background.new: The 2026 estimates quantify the combined growth, export and daily financing pressure ahead of winter.

left.label: Scale
left.text: Officials estimate $10 billion of 2026 damage and $40 billion of export revenue exposed by port disruption.

right.label: Measurement limit
right.text: Wartime accounts are provisional, and exposed revenue is not the same as revenue already lost.

sources.label: Reuters · Ukraine's winter economic and fiscal squeeze
Reuters · latest attacks on cities, ships and plants

stories.title: BRICS agreed to connect national payment systems and expand local-currency finance, without creating a common currency.
stories.changed: The 11 BRICS members adopted the New Delhi Declaration by consensus. It condemns unilateral sanctions, tariffs and attacks on civilian and safeguarded nuclear facilities. Economically, it directs a Payment Task Force to improve interoperability among national messaging and payment systems, encourages local-currency trade and investment, and backs more local-currency lending by the New Development Bank. The document explicitly says there is no one-size-fits-all approach and does not announce a BRICS currency.
stories.matters: The practical strategy is incremental resilience rather than a dramatic replacement for the dollar. Connecting domestic rails, settling more bilateral trade in local currencies and financing projects without dollar liabilities can reduce friction when sanctions or correspondent banks interrupt transactions. But interoperability creates governance, liquidity and convertibility problems of its own. Consensus among members including Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE is politically notable; operational adoption will be the harder test.
stories.watch: Technical standards and pilot corridors from the Payment Task Force; participating banks; settlement volumes rather than announcements; currency-swap lines; New Development Bank issuance; fraud and dispute rules; sanctions exposure; and whether geopolitical consensus survives implementation choices that distribute costs unevenly.

group.label: Global economic architecture
group.title: The bloc chose connective plumbing over a symbolic new currency.
group.note: The declaration is a political commitment. It does not establish convertibility, common monetary policy or material transaction volume.

background.title: Payments can diversify without a shared currency
background.text: A cross-border transaction needs messaging, settlement assets, liquidity, compliance and a process for reversing errors or resolving disputes. Countries can link national systems and invoice in their own currencies without pooling sovereignty in a common currency. This can reduce exposure to a single correspondent network, but it shifts risk toward exchange rates, local liquidity and fragmented rules. The New Delhi approach is therefore technically plausible and institutionally demanding. Its success will be visible in routine corporate use, not summit language.
background.known: BRICS members have promoted local-currency trade and New Development Bank financing for several years.
background.new: All 11 members endorsed a specific workstream on payment and messaging interoperability while avoiding a common-currency promise.

left.label: Concrete mandate
left.text: The declaration assigns payment interoperability to a task force and supports more local-currency financing.

right.label: Missing execution
right.text: No shared currency, launch date, transaction target or unified legal framework was adopted.

sources.label: Government of India · New Delhi Declaration
AP · summit context and member differences

stories.title: Modi and Xi declared India and China partners rather than rivals, but left the border dispute unresolved.
stories.changed: Xi Jinping visited India for the first time since 2019 and met Narendra Modi alongside the BRICS summit. Both leaders described stable relations and border peace as essential, discussed trade imbalance, market access and supply-chain predictability, and said they should treat each other as development partners rather than threats. Their statements offered no new border settlement, disengagement timetable or enforceable commercial concession.
stories.matters: The meeting lowers the political temperature between the two largest BRICS economies at a moment both want insulation from U.S. tariffs and war-driven disruption. A durable reset could restore investment, tourism and supply-chain links and give BRICS more internal coherence. Yet the relationship's binding constraints are territorial and structural. Diplomatic language can reopen working channels; it cannot substitute for verified border arrangements or reciprocal market access.
stories.watch: Military deployments and patrol agreements at the disputed border; direct flights and visas; Chinese investment approvals; Indian restrictions on technology firms; trade-deficit measures; leader-level follow-up; and whether cooperation inside BRICS survives new security or market-access disputes.

group.label: Strategic reset
group.title: The rhetoric changed faster than the underlying constraints.
group.note: The leaders' alignment is official. It is an opening for negotiation, not evidence that the border or trade disputes are solved.

background.title: Political normalization and strategic trust move on different clocks
background.text: India and China can restore flights, visas, ministerial dialogue and commercial approvals relatively quickly. Border trust is harder because it depends on deployments, patrol behavior, maps and verification across disputed terrain. Trade is similarly asymmetric: India wants market access and reliable inputs while seeking to reduce dependence in sensitive sectors. A reset can be economically valuable before full trust returns, but that same partial interdependence is vulnerable to the next security incident.
background.known: Relations deteriorated after the 2020 border clash and only recently began a cautious thaw.
background.new: Xi returned to India and both leaders publicly adopted a partners-not-rivals frame tied to border peace and economic cooperation.

left.label: Political signal
left.text: The first Xi visit since 2019 and coordinated language indicate deliberate normalization.

right.label: Substantive gap
right.text: No new border disposition, implementation timetable or enforceable market-access measure was disclosed.

sources.label: AP · Modi-Xi meeting and unresolved issues
Xinhua · official Chinese account of the meeting

stories.title: Anthropic proposed slowing frontier development and embedding outside evaluators; rivals are beginning to support the mechanism.
stories.changed: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei proposed that leading AI labs pace capability development, grant independent evaluators on-site access with desks, credentials, laptops and permissions, publish findings with narrow redactions, and coordinate under government-backed antitrust safeguards. He argued that autonomous cyber misuse could reach dangerous scale within six to 12 months, a forecast rather than an observed fact. Sam Altman separately supported embedded evaluation and an industry pact, while saying an OpenAI listing would not occur in 2026.
stories.matters: The important proposal is access. Public model cards and benchmark scores are chosen and mediated by the developer; embedded evaluators could inspect systems, processes and incident evidence that outsiders cannot reproduce. A shared pacing agreement might reduce pressure to conceal risk, but it could also protect incumbents, leak secrets or become theatre without enforcement. Convergence among competitors makes the mechanism more plausible while leaving governance, independence and international participation unresolved.
stories.watch: Named evaluator institutions; access rights and publication rules; funding independence; treatment of proprietary and classified information; government antitrust waivers; measurable pause or pacing thresholds; participation by Chinese labs; incident disclosure; and whether companies accept findings that delay release.

group.label: AI and technology
group.title: Safety debate is moving from promises toward inspection rights.
group.note: The governance proposal is concrete. The six-to-12-month cyber forecast is Amodei's judgment, not a verified timetable.

background.title: An evaluator is only independent if access, incentives and publication rights survive bad news
background.text: A lab can commission an external test while controlling the model version, questions, timing and disclosure. Embedding evaluators can reduce that information gap by giving them continuing access to staff, systems and incidents. It also creates new conflicts: the evaluator may depend on the lab for funding and credentials, while broad access raises security and intellectual-property risk. A credible arrangement therefore needs selection rules, protected budgets, minimum access, publication presumptions and a path for escalation when the company disagrees.
background.known: Frontier labs already run internal and selected external evaluations, and competitive pressure rewards rapid release.
background.new: A leading lab CEO is asking for persistent embedded access and coordinated pacing, with a rival CEO endorsing the broad mechanism.

left.label: Institutional advance
left.text: The proposal specifies physical and technical access, disclosure and competition-law support rather than relying on voluntary principles alone.

right.label: Open design
right.text: No evaluator, binding threshold, enforcement body or global membership has yet been agreed.

sources.label: Dario Amodei · proposal to pace the frontier
AP · proposal, forecasts and industry response
Fortune · Altman on embedded evaluation and an industry pact

radar.label: Qatar diplomacy
radar.title: Qatar and Kuwait coordinated on maritime navigation and a comprehensive regional settlement.
radar.text: The call reinforces Qatar's public position without announcing a new mediation channel or operational guarantee. Watch whether Monday's Oman meeting produces a mechanism that Qatar supports or helps implement.

radar.label: Travel and hospitality
radar.title: August U.S. airfares rose 2.7% and lodging rose 2.4% in one month.
radar.text: These are national price indices, not proof of stronger volumes. The combination suggests constrained capacity and energy costs are reaching the travel basket faster than restaurant prices.

radar.label: Yemen humanitarian risk
radar.title: The latest Houthi advance has displaced an estimated 85,000 people since September began.
radar.text: AP reports more than 2,000 people crossed to Djibouti as fighting moved around Mokha and Bab el-Mandeb. Aid access and independently verified control remain the immediate tests.

attention.title: The Saudi pipeline shutdown as a test of Gulf redundancy
attention.text: Read the official Saudi accounts together with the Houthi and Hormuz reporting. The useful question is not whether one chokepoint is closed, but how much capacity remains when land, terminal and maritime risks become correlated.

ignore.title: Calling Monday's Oman meeting a reopening of Hormuz
ignore.text: Iran says the talks concern traffic management and possible fees, not an unconditional reopening; commercial traffic remains low and key attendance is not yet universal.

history.title: The digital world began when engineers learned not only to invent the transistor, but to manufacture millions of reliable ones together.
history.deck: Bell Labs demonstrated the first transistor in 1947, replacing fragile vacuum-tube switching with a tiny solid-state device. Yet early transistors were handcrafted, exposed and difficult to connect. The decisive manufacturing shift came a decade later at Fairchild Semiconductor. Jean Hoerni's planar process built components beneath a protective silicon-dioxide layer; Robert Noyce realized the same surface could carry metal interconnections, turning separate devices into a practical monolithic integrated circuit. Photolithography made the pattern repeatable, Apollo created demanding early demand, and Gordon Moore described the economic loop in which more components per chip lowered the cost of each function and financed the next generation of equipment. The lesson is larger than computing: invention creates possibility, but a manufacturing process creates scale.
history.thesis: The transistor changed technology only after the planar process made reliability, interconnection and mass replication part of the same system.

sections.title: The first transistor proved the principle, not the production model
sections.text: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley demonstrated transistor action at Bell Labs in December 1947. The device could amplify and switch electrical signals without the heat, size and frequent failure of vacuum tubes. The three later received the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics. But early point-contact and junction transistors required delicate fabrication and packaging. They established that semiconductors could control current; they did not yet offer a cheap route to place thousands of dependable devices in one machine.

sections.title: A protective oxide layer became the factory's organizing surface
sections.text: At Fairchild Semiconductor, Jean Hoerni developed the planar process in 1959. Engineers had often removed silicon dioxide after using it as a mask during diffusion. Hoerni kept the oxide on the wafer, protecting sensitive junctions from contamination while openings allowed precisely placed electrical contacts. Components could now be formed from one side of a flat silicon surface using repeated masking, oxidation, diffusion and etching steps. Fairchild demonstrated the process in 1959 and sold planar transistors commercially in 1960.

sections.title: Noyce turned the planar surface into an integrated circuit
sections.text: Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments demonstrated an integrated circuit in 1958, proving that multiple circuit elements could share one piece of semiconductor. His prototype still depended on fine external wires. Robert Noyce saw that Hoerni's oxide layer could insulate metal lines deposited directly across the chip, joining components while the planar process created them. His 1959 concept made the monolithic integrated circuit compatible with batch manufacturing. Kilby and Noyce supplied complementary breakthroughs: integration as an idea and integration as a scalable process.

sections.title: Photolithography made complexity reproducible
sections.text: A circuit design could be reduced to patterned masks, projected onto light-sensitive material and repeated across a wafer. Each process step acted on many devices at once; the wafer was then divided into individual chips. Manufacturing economics changed because the cost of a step was shared across every working chip and every component on it. Yield became decisive: dust, alignment errors or material defects could ruin a die, so clean rooms, measurement and process control mattered as much as circuit design.

sections.title: Apollo bought reliability before consumer markets bought abundance
sections.text: The Apollo Guidance Computer used integrated circuits when the technology was still expensive and immature. The space programme needed low weight, modest power use and consistent behavior under severe constraints, creating an early customer willing to pay for reliability. Large, disciplined orders helped manufacturers improve yield and reduce cost. Defense and aerospace demand did not by itself create the later consumer industry, but it gave the process a proving ground while calculators, computers and communications markets grew.

sections.title: Moore's observation described an economic flywheel, not a law of nature
sections.text: In 1965, Gordon Moore observed that the number of components on economical integrated circuits had roughly doubled each year and argued the trend could continue. More density reduced the cost of a function, expanding demand; larger markets financed better tools, cleaner factories and new designs; those investments enabled still more density. The cadence later slowed, and physical scaling has become harder and more expensive. The durable insight is the feedback loop. Today's chips depend on global suppliers, extreme-ultraviolet lithography, advanced packaging and vast capital budgets—the modern complements to Hoerni's flat protected surface.

timeline.text: Bell Labs demonstrates the first working transistor.
Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley receive the Nobel Prize in Physics.
Jack Kilby demonstrates an integrated circuit at Texas Instruments.
Jean Hoerni develops the planar process at Fairchild Semiconductor.
Robert Noyce proposes planar metal interconnections for a monolithic circuit.
Fairchild begins commercial production of planar transistors.
Gordon Moore publishes his component-density forecast.
Apollo 11 flies with an integrated-circuit guidance computer.
